title: This is what my screen looks like today, I'm pretty excited!
author: strawberry-ramune
selftext: Every window is its own copy of the game, and each one has an AI agent working on a different piece of it. As I watch each instance go through it's tests, I'm sending instructions and design info over to claude so it can add them to the work queue. There's a lot of pieces that all have to come together, but so far it's coming together really smoothly! I'm pretty excited!

comments.author: vala_ai
comments.body:
Looks really interesting. I like the style of your game as well :)  
  
You have this all running on one machine correct? How do the agents not conflict when working on potentially overlapping features? More info on how you set it up would be great.

replies.author: TheJotaErre_Twitch
replies.body: Me imagino porque usan copias del juego y luego las junta para volver a partir de ahí puede ser?

replies.author: strawberry-ramune
replies.body: Exactly, each subagent works on it's own copy. When the work is done the new files get pulled over into the main one.

replies.author: strawberry-ramune
replies.body:
Yes, everything runs on one machine! When an agent is spun up, it gets a list of the files it's allowed to work on and a prompt that gives it the goals and the expected results.  

Most of the work is editing script files, and each running copy has the full command suite, so any normal instruction you can send through the console can be scripted by the agent. For every feature added, the agent writes a test, and then uses screenshots and returned data to check that the feature works as expected. Each test run launches its own copy of the game, with its own window, port and save folder, so agents testing at the same time don't interfere.  
  
When they're finished, they run the full test suite, so if anything broke, they can see the errors. 

If the agent spots a problem in a file it doesn't own, it reports the issue back to a coordinator agent. The coordinator passes it to the agent that owns that file, which fixes it and runs its own tests. Then the first agent re-tests to confirm.

comments.author: FocusKontrol
comments.body: I’ve been thinking of something like this on my system with Unreal, but there’s limitations that when one agent wants to build from IDE or do PIE test, they block other agents from using MCP tools. How do you work around that?

replies.author: strawberry-ramune
replies.body:
Our engine was set up from the beginning to run and control the game independently of an IDE. Each agent launches a separate standalone game process with its own command endpoint, port, saves, and logs. Commands target a specific instance ID, so agents aren’t competing to control one editor.

Each instance gets a snapshot of the built executable, libraries, and resources. Agents can run test scripts against their instance or send commands directly to drive the game, use its in-game editor tools, and read back results. Game scripts and authored files still live in a shared source tree, so a coordinator assigns file ownership to avoid conflicting edits.

Hopefully this answers your question!

replies.author: FocusKontrol
replies.body: What engine are you using? Or are you using your own?

replies.author: strawberry-ramune
replies.body:
I’m using Fenris Creations’ open-sourced Carbon framework as the native foundation. It’s C++ with a built-in Python layer. It provides the renderer, scheduler, and low level networking. Most of what you see is Python that I built on top of it. 

There’s no editor like Unreal has, instead I built the game to be its own editor where maps, objects, modeling etc is all handled within the game application, and every control inside is accessible by a command line. Game logic is done with Python and animations have their own custom scripting language, similar to Renpy ATL. 

I can give AI simple prompts like “fill this room out with furniture” or “make a cinematic of this scene where x y z happens” and the AI has everything it needs built right into the game.

comments.author: SpicyBoyEnthusiast
comments.body: What Claude plan do you have? What prompt did you do for getting it to run five tests at once and watch them?

replies.author: strawberry-ramune
replies.body: I have the $100 Claude plan and I usually hit my weekly cap in 3-4 days. As for the process, I talk about it a bit in the other comments. Basically use subagents, and make your game in such a way that it can receive commands from a CLI. Then just point each agent to the right process ID.
